records.source: Ἔλεγεν δὲ καὶ πρὸς τοὺς μαθητάς· Ἄνθρωπός τις ἦν πλούσιος ὃς εἶχεν οἰκονόμον, καὶ οὗτος διεβλήθη αὐτῷ ὡς διασκορπίζων τὰ ὑπάρχοντα αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: He was saying now also to the disciples, A man certain there was rich who had a manager, and he was accused to him as wasting the possessions of him.
pieces: Jesus also told the disciples this: "A rich man had a manager, and word reached him that this man was squandering what he owned.

L.1: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was also saying to the disciples, "There was a certain rich man who had a manager, and this [manager] was accused to him of wasting his possessions.

R.1: Jesus also told {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples this story: "There was once a rich man who had a manager to look after his property. Someone told the rich man that the manager was wasting his money.

decisions.choice: manager: a steward who ran a rich man's estate and business for him
alternatives: a household slave with no authority
decisions.reason: A manager could make contracts, lend goods and collect debts in his master's name (12:42). Here he has charge of what the rich man owns and of the accounts of those who owe him.

decisions.choice: was accused: was reported, charged with wrongdoing
decisions.reason: The verb is often used of a hostile report, sometimes a false one. The manager does not deny it, and 16:8 calls him dishonest.

decisions.choice: wasting: scattering, letting it slip away
decisions.reason: The same verb is used of the younger son in 15:13. The charge is careless or wasteful handling of his master's goods.

decisions.choice: also to the disciples: the same audience as chapter 15, with the disciples now addressed
decisions.reason: "Also" links this parable with the three before it. The Pharisees are still listening (16:14).

decisions.choice: to look after his property; Someone told the rich man
alternatives: a manager; was accused to him
decisions.reason: Readable says what a manager did and turns the passive into a plain sentence.

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and runs on to 16:13; the speakers' words are in single quotation marks
alternatives: a quotation for the parable only
decisions.reason: The parable and the sayings after it (16:8-13) are one speech of Jesus.

records.heading: A manager who acted shrewdly

records.source: καὶ φωνήσας αὐτὸν εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Τί τοῦτο ἀκούω περὶ σοῦ;
records.gloss: And having called him he said to him, What [is] this I hear concerning you?
pieces: So he sent for him and said, 'What is this that I keep hearing about you?

L.2: And calling him, he said to him, 'What is this I hear about you?

R.2: So he called the manager in and said to him, 'I have heard things about you. What is going on?

decisions.choice: What is this I hear: a demand for an answer, not a request for news
decisions.reason: The question already assumes the report is true. The next sentence dismisses him.

decisions.choice: a statement, then the question
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the question into two short sentences.

decisions.choice: his words open here and run on to 16:2b
decisions.reason: The master's words are one speech.

records.source: ἀπόδος τὸν λόγον τῆς οἰκονομίας σου, οὐ γὰρ δύνῃ ἔτι οἰκονομεῖν.
records.gloss: Give the account of the stewardship of you, not for you are able any longer to manage.
pieces: Hand in a report on how you have managed my affairs, because you cannot be my manager any longer.'

L.2: Give the account of your management, for you can no longer manage.'

R.2: Give me a full report of the work you have done for me. You cannot be my manager anymore.'

decisions.choice: give the account of your management: hand over the accounts, so that the estate can pass to someone else
decisions.reason: "Account" here is a business record. He is to give up the books before he goes.

decisions.choice: you can no longer manage: you are dismissed
alternatives: you are not able to do the work
decisions.reason: The master has decided. The manager has only a short time before he must leave.

records.source: εἶπεν δὲ ἐν ἑαυτῷ ὁ οἰκονόμος· Τί ποιήσω ὅτι ὁ κύριός μου ἀφαιρεῖται τὴν οἰκονομίαν ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ;
records.gloss: Said then within himself the manager, What shall I do, for the master of me is taking away the management from me?
pieces: The manager thought it over: 'My master is taking my position from me. What am I to do?

L.3: And the manager said within himself, 'What shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me?

R.3: The manager thought to himself, 'What can I do? My master is going to take my job away from me.

decisions.choice: said within himself: thought to himself
decisions.reason: Luke often lets readers hear a person's thoughts this way (12:17; 15:17-19).

decisions.choice: master: the rich man in the parable
decisions.reason: The word can mean "lord" or "master". In the parable it is the owner of the estate, as in 12:42-46.

decisions.choice: the reason first, then the question
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the cause first; the meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: his thoughts open here and run on to 16:4
decisions.reason: The manager's thoughts are one speech to himself.

records.source: σκάπτειν οὐκ ἰσχύω, ἐπαιτεῖν αἰσχύνομαι·
records.gloss: To dig not I am able, to beg I am ashamed.
pieces: Digging is too hard for me, and I would be ashamed to beg.

L.3: I am not strong enough to dig; I am ashamed to beg.

R.3: I am not strong enough to work digging in the fields. And I would be too ashamed to beg for money.

decisions.choice: to dig; to beg: the work of the poorest laborers, and the life of those who could not work
decisions.reason: Digging was hard work for day laborers. A man who had lived as a manager would not have the strength for it, and begging would shame him.

decisions.choice: I am not able: I am not strong enough
decisions.reason: The verb means to have strength.

decisions.choice: in the fields; for money
decisions.reason: Readable fills out the two pictures.

records.source: ἔγνων τί ποιήσω, ἵνα ὅταν μετασταθῶ ἐκ τῆς οἰκονομίας δέξωνταί με εἰς τοὺς οἴκους ἑαυτῶν.
records.gloss: I know what I will do, so that when I shall have been removed from the management, they might receive me into the homes of them.
pieces: Now I know what I will do, so that when I am put out of my job, people will open their homes to me.'

L.4: I know what I will do, so that when I am removed from the management, they may receive me into their homes.'

R.4: I know what I will do! Then, when I lose my job, people will be my friends and welcome me into their homes.'

decisions.choice: I know: a sudden idea, "I have it"
decisions.reason: The verb form describes a moment of decision: the plan comes to him all at once.

decisions.choice: they: the people who owe his master, as 16:5 shows
decisions.reason: The Greek does not say who will receive him. The next verses show whom he means.

decisions.choice: receive me into their homes: give him a place and support, as people do for one who has done them a favor
decisions.reason: In that world a favor put the one who received it under obligation to repay. The manager makes friends who will owe him.

decisions.choice: people
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable avoid a "they" with nothing before it to refer to.

records.source: καὶ προσκαλεσάμενος ἕνα ἕκαστον τῶν χρεοφειλετῶν τοῦ κυρίου ἑαυτοῦ ἔλεγεν τῷ πρώτῳ· Πόσον ὀφείλεις τῷ κυρίῳ μου;
records.gloss: And having called to [him] one each of the debtors of the master of himself he was saying to the first, How much owe you to the master of me?
pieces: He sent for his master's debtors one by one. To the first he said, 'How much do you owe my master?'

L.5: And calling to [him] each one of his own master's debtors, he said to the first, 'How much do you owe my master?'

R.5: So he called in all the people who owed his master something, one at a time. He asked the first one, 'How much do you owe my master?'

decisions.choice: debtors: tenants or traders who owed the estate goods, often a share of the harvest
alternatives: people who had borrowed money at interest
decisions.reason: Debts were often counted in produce: oil and wheat in the next verses. Tenant farmers paid rent in kind, and merchants might owe for goods received.

decisions.choice: one each: one at a time
decisions.reason: He deals with each debtor alone, so that each owes the favor to him.

records.source: ὁ δὲ εἶπεν· Ἑκατὸν βάτους ἐλαίου· ὁ δὲ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Δέξαι σου τὰ γράμματα καὶ καθίσας ταχέως γράψον πεντήκοντα.
records.gloss: He and said, A hundred baths of oil. He and said to him, Take your the bill and having sat down quickly write fifty.
pieces: '{{units:About 600 gallons|A hundred baths}} of olive oil,' he answered. The manager told him, 'Here is your bill. Sit down quickly and write {{units:300 gallons|fifty}}.'

L.6: And he said, 'A hundred baths of oil.' And he said to him, 'Take your bill, and sit down quickly [and] write fifty.'

R.6: The man answered, '{{units:About 600 gallons|A hundred baths}} of olive oil.' The manager said to him, 'Take your bill. Sit down quickly and change it to {{units:300 gallons|fifty baths}}.'

decisions.choice: a hundred baths of oil: a large debt of olive oil
alternatives: a small amount for one household
decisions.reason: The bath was a Hebrew measure for liquids (1 Kings 7:26; Ezekiel 45:10-14). Its size is not known exactly: a jar marked as a bath found in Judah held about 22 liters (about 6 gallons), while Josephus suggests a larger measure. A hundred baths is roughly 2,200 liters or more, the yield of a large olive grove.

decisions.choice: bill: the written agreement or note of the debt
decisions.reason: The word means writings, here the document that recorded what the debtor owed. The debtor writes the new figure in his own hand.

decisions.choice: fifty: he cuts the debt in half
decisions.reason: The manager has the debtor change the amount on the bill. Whether he was removing his own commission, the interest, or simply his master's goods, the text does not say; 16:8 calls him dishonest.

decisions.choice: {{units:About 600 gallons|A hundred baths}}; {{units:300 gallons|fifty}} (B), {{units:300 gallons|fifty baths}} (R)
alternatives: a hundred baths at every level
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give a modern measure by default, with the original measure as the alternative. Literal keeps the bath. The figure follows the smaller, better-attested size of the bath; a larger estimate would give about 800 or 900 gallons.

decisions.choice: olive oil
decisions.reason: The oil of that land was olive oil.

decisions.choice: change it to
decisions.reason: Readable says what writing the new figure meant.

records.source: ἔπειτα ἑτέρῳ εἶπεν· Σὺ δὲ πόσον ὀφείλεις;
records.gloss: Then to another he said, You now how much owe?
pieces: Then he said to another, 'And what do you owe?'

L.7: Then to another he said, 'And you, how much do you owe?'

R.7: Then he asked another man, 'How much do you owe?'

decisions.choice: another: a second debtor, one example of the many
decisions.reason: Two examples show what he did with each debtor (16:5).

records.source: ὁ δὲ εἶπεν· Ἑκατὸν κόρους σίτου· λέγει αὐτῷ· Δέξαι σου τὰ γράμματα καὶ γράψον ὀγδοήκοντα.
records.gloss: He and said, A hundred cors of wheat. He says to him, Take your the bill and write eighty.
pieces: '{{units:About 600 bushels|A hundred cors}} of wheat,' he replied. The manager told him, 'Take your bill and write {{units:about 500|eighty}}.'

L.7: And he said, 'A hundred cors of wheat.' He says to him, 'Take your bill and write eighty.'

R.7: '{{units:About 600 bushels|A hundred cors}} of wheat,' the man said. The manager told him, 'Take your bill and change it to {{units:about 500 bushels|eighty cors}}.'

decisions.choice: a hundred cors of wheat: a very large debt of grain
decisions.reason: The cor was the largest Hebrew dry measure, equal to ten baths (Ezekiel 45:14). On the measure of about 22 liters for a bath, a hundred cors is about 22,000 liters, the harvest of a large farm. Like the oil in 16:6, the size is uncertain.

decisions.choice: eighty: he cuts the debt by a fifth
decisions.reason: Twenty cors of wheat was a large sum, perhaps close in value to the fifty baths of oil.

decisions.choice: {{units:About 600 bushels|A hundred cors}}; {{units:about 500|eighty}} (B), {{units:about 500 bushels|eighty cors}} (R)
alternatives: a hundred cors at every level
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give a modern measure by default, with the original measure as the alternative, on the same size of bath as 16:6. Literal keeps the cor.

decisions.choice: The manager
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker.

decisions.choice: change it to
decisions.reason: As in 16:6.

records.source: καὶ ἐπῄνεσεν ὁ κύριος τὸν οἰκονόμον τῆς ἀδικίας ὅτι φρονίμως ἐποίησεν· ὅτι οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου φρονιμώτεροι ὑπὲρ τοὺς υἱοὺς τοῦ φωτὸς εἰς τὴν γενεὰν τὴν ἑαυτῶν εἰσιν.
records.gloss: And praised the master the manager of unrighteousness because shrewdly he had acted; for the sons of the age this more shrewd than the sons of the light toward the generation of themselves are.
pieces: So the master gave the dishonest manager credit for acting so shrewdly. For the people of this age deal more shrewdly with others of their own kind than the people of the light do.

L.8: And the master praised the manager of unrighteousness because he had acted shrewdly; for the {{gender:children|sons}} of this age are more shrewd toward their own generation than the {{gender:children|sons}} of the light.

R.8: When the master heard about it, he praised the dishonest manager for being so clever. People who belong to this world are wiser in dealing with each other than people who belong to the light.

decisions.choice: the master: the rich man in the parable
decisions.reason: The word is the one used for the master in 16:3 and 16:5, so it most likely means the same man. Some take it as Luke's name for Jesus (as in 18:6), which would make Jesus the one who praises. The verse goes on to Jesus' own comment.

decisions.choice: manager of unrighteousness: the dishonest manager
alternatives: a manager of a wicked master
decisions.reason: "Of unrighteousness" describes the manager, a Hebrew way of saying "unrighteous" (compare 18:6, "judge of unrighteousness").

decisions.choice: shrewdly: with practical wisdom, thinking ahead
decisions.reason: The master praises his foresight, not his dishonesty. The same word describes the wise manager in 12:42.

decisions.choice: the sons of this age; the sons of the light: people who belong to this present world, and people who belong to God
decisions.reason: "Son of" was a Hebrew way of saying that a person belonged to or shared the nature of something (10:6; John 12:36; 1 Thessalonians 5:5). Jewish writings of the time also speak of the sons of light.

decisions.choice: toward their own generation: in dealing with people of their own kind
decisions.reason: People of this world are clever in their dealings with one another; Jesus' followers should be as wise in their own way.

decisions.choice: {{gender:children|sons}}
decisions.reason: The phrase means people of both sexes, as in 6:35.

decisions.choice: the people of this age; the people of the light (B); people who belong to this world; people who belong to the light (R)
alternatives: sons of this age; sons of the light
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the idiom.

decisions.choice: When the master heard about it
decisions.reason: Readable supplies how the master came to know, which the story implies.

records.source: καὶ ἐγὼ ὑμῖν λέγω, ἑαυτοῖς ποιήσατε φίλους ἐκ τοῦ μαμωνᾶ τῆς ἀδικίας, ἵνα ὅταν ἐκλίπῃ δέξωνται ὑμᾶς εἰς τὰς αἰωνίους σκηνάς.
records.gloss: And I to you say, for yourselves make friends by the mammon of unrighteousness, that when it fails they might receive you into the eternal dwellings.
pieces: And I tell you, use the wealth of this unjust world to make friends for yourselves, so that when it is gone, they will welcome you into the eternal homes.

L.9: And I say to you, make friends for yourselves by means of the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.

R.9: I tell you, use the money of this unfair world to make friends for yourselves. Then when your money is gone, you will be welcomed into eternal homes.

decisions.choice: mammon: wealth, money and possessions
alternatives: a god or demon named Mammon
decisions.reason: The word is Aramaic for wealth or what a person owns. In 16:13 it is pictured as a master who competes with God, but it is not the name of a god.

decisions.choice: the mammon of unrighteousness: wealth that belongs to this unjust world
decisions.reason: As with "the manager of unrighteousness" (16:8), the phrase is a Hebrew way of describing. Wealth easily leads people into wrong and belongs to this passing age, unlike the true riches of 16:11. Jesus does not mean only money gained dishonestly.

decisions.choice: when it fails: when wealth runs out or comes to an end, at death or at the end of this age
decisions.reason: The subject is the wealth. Like the manager's position, money will not last.

decisions.choice: when it fails (SBLGNT)
alternatives: when you fail, that is, when you die
decisions.reason: The earliest manuscripts read "when it fails". Many later manuscripts read "when you fail", meaning when you die. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: they may receive you: the friends made by generous giving, or God
decisions.reason: The friends are the poor who have been helped (compare 12:33; 14:13-14). The plural can also be a reverent way of speaking of God's action, as in 12:20.

decisions.choice: the eternal dwellings: homes in the life of the age to come
decisions.reason: The word means tents or dwellings. In contrast to the homes the manager hoped for (16:4), these last forever.

decisions.choice: mammon (L); wealth (B); money (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "mammon", the Aramaic word for wealth that the Greek itself borrows. Balanced says "wealth" and Readable "money", the everyday words for it.

decisions.choice: of this unjust world (B); of this unfair world (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the Hebrew-style phrase, as the meaning decision explains.

decisions.choice: you will be welcomed
decisions.reason: Readable leaves the welcomers unnamed, as the Greek leaves them unclear.

records.source: Ὁ πιστὸς ἐν ἐλαχίστῳ καὶ ἐν πολλῷ πιστός ἐστιν, καὶ ὁ ἐν ἐλαχίστῳ ἄδικος καὶ ἐν πολλῷ ἄδικός ἐστιν.
records.gloss: The [one] faithful with very little also with much faithful is, and the [one] with very little unrighteous also with much unrighteous is.
pieces: Someone who is faithful in the smallest matter is faithful in large matters too, and someone who is dishonest in the smallest matter is dishonest in large matters too.

L.10: The one faithful in very little is also faithful in much, and the one unrighteous in very little is also unrighteous in much.

R.10: If people can be trusted with small things, they can be trusted with big things too. If people are dishonest with small things, they will be dishonest with big things too.

decisions.choice: faithful: reliable, able to be trusted
decisions.reason: The word describes someone who does what is entrusted to him, as in 12:42.

decisions.choice: unrighteous: dishonest, unjust
decisions.reason: The opposite of faithful here. It picks up the "manager of unrighteousness" (16:8).

decisions.choice: a general saying about character
decisions.reason: How a person handles small things shows how he will handle great ones. The next verses apply it to wealth.

decisions.choice: can be trusted
decisions.reason: Readable uses the everyday meaning of the word.

records.source: εἰ οὖν ἐν τῷ ἀδίκῳ μαμωνᾷ πιστοὶ οὐκ ἐγένεσθε, τὸ ἀληθινὸν τίς ὑμῖν πιστεύσει;
records.gloss: If therefore in the unrighteous mammon faithful not you have been, the true [riches] who to you will entrust?
pieces: So if you have not been faithful in handling unjust wealth, who will put real wealth in your care?

L.11: If, then, you have not been faithful with the unrighteous mammon, who will entrust the true [riches] to you?

R.11: So if you cannot be trusted with the money of this unfair world, who will trust you with the riches that really matter?

decisions.choice: will entrust: will put in your care
decisions.reason: The verb usually means to believe or trust in. With an object handed over, it means to entrust something to someone.

decisions.choice: the true riches: what has real and lasting worth, the riches of God's kingdom
decisions.reason: The word means true or real, in contrast to wealth that passes away (12:33).

decisions.choice: the unrighteous mammon: wealth that belongs to this unjust world
decisions.reason: As in 16:9.

decisions.choice: mammon (L); wealth (B); money (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "mammon", the Aramaic word for wealth that the Greek itself borrows. Balanced says "wealth" and Readable "money", the everyday words for it.

decisions.choice: entrust (L); put in your care (B); trust you with (R)
decisions.reason: The verb here means to entrust, as the meaning decision explains.

decisions.choice: [riches] (L); wealth (B); riches (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "the true"; the context supplies the noun.

records.source: καὶ εἰ ἐν τῷ ἀλλοτρίῳ πιστοὶ οὐκ ἐγένεσθε, τὸ ὑμέτερον τίς δώσει ὑμῖν;
records.gloss: And if in that which [is] another's faithful not you have been, that which [is] yours who will give to you?
pieces: And if you have not proved faithful with what is another's, who will hand you what is your own?

L.12: And if you have not been faithful with what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?

R.12: And if you cannot be trusted with things that belong to someone else, who will give you things of your own?

decisions.choice: what belongs to another: wealth in this life, held in trust from God
decisions.reason: Like the manager, people only manage what they have for a time. Their own lasting riches are still to come.

decisions.choice: yours (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Most manuscripts read "yours". A few, among them Codex Vaticanus, read "ours", which would mean the riches that belong to God and Jesus. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

records.source: οὐδεὶς οἰκέτης δύναται δυσὶ κυρίοις δουλεύειν· ἢ γὰρ τὸν ἕνα μισήσει καὶ τὸν ἕτερον ἀγαπήσει, ἢ ἑνὸς ἀνθέξεται καὶ τοῦ ἑτέρου καταφρονήσει.
records.gloss: No household servant is able two masters to serve, either for the one he will hate and the other he will love, or one he will be devoted to and the other he will despise.
pieces: No servant in a household can serve two masters. Either the servant will hate one master and love the other, or be loyal to one and look down on the other.

L.13: No household servant can serve two masters as a slave; for either {{gender:they|he}} will hate the one and love the other, or {{gender:they|he}} will hold to one and despise the other.

R.13: A servant cannot serve two masters at the same time. That servant will hate one master and love the other. Or the servant will be loyal to one and not care about the other.

decisions.choice: household servant; to serve as a slave: one who belongs to a master and works for him alone
alternatives: a hired worker who could have two employers
decisions.reason: The first word is a servant of the household, usually a slave. The verb is formed from the word for a slave. A slave belonged wholly to one owner.

decisions.choice: hate ... love: reject one and choose the other
decisions.reason: In Hebrew speech "love" and "hate" can mean choosing one over the other (Genesis 29:30-31; Malachi 1:2-3; Luke 14:26).

decisions.choice: hold to; despise: be loyal to one, and think little of the other
decisions.reason: The two verbs describe loyalty and disregard.

decisions.choice: {{gender:they|he}}
decisions.reason: The saying is about any servant, man or woman.

decisions.choice: the servant
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable repeat the noun instead of a pronoun.

decisions.choice: serve
decisions.reason: "Serve" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it for the slave words and as in Matthew 6:24; the meaning decision (m1) keeps that a slave belonged wholly to one owner, and Literal keeps "serve as a slave".

records.source: οὐ δύνασθε θεῷ δουλεύειν καὶ μαμωνᾷ.
records.gloss: Not you are able God to serve and mammon.
pieces: You cannot serve both God and wealth."

L.13: You cannot serve God and mammon as a slave serves."

R.13: You cannot serve God and money at the same time."

decisions.choice: God and mammon: wealth pictured as a master that demands a person's loyalty
decisions.reason: Wealth is not a god, but it can rule a life as a master rules a slave. A person must choose whom to serve (12:15; 18:22-25).

decisions.choice: mammon (L); wealth (B); money (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "mammon", the Aramaic word for wealth that the Greek itself borrows. Balanced says "wealth" and Readable "money", the everyday words for it.

decisions.choice: the quotation closes here
decisions.reason: Luke's words in 16:14 interrupt Jesus' speech.

decisions.choice: serve
decisions.reason: "Serve" in Balanced and Readable, as in the first half of the saying (16:13) and in Matthew 6:24; Literal keeps "as a slave serves".

records.source: Ἤκουον δὲ ταῦτα πάντα οἱ Φαρισαῖοι φιλάργυροι ὑπάρχοντες, καὶ ἐξεμυκτήριζον αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Were listening to now these things all the Pharisees, lovers of money being, and they were ridiculing him.
pieces: The Pharisees were listening to all this. They loved money, and they turned up their noses at {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.14: Now the Pharisees, being lovers of money, were listening to all these things, and they were sneering at {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.14: The Pharisees heard everything Jesus said. They loved money, so they made fun of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: the Pharisees: a Jewish movement devoted to keeping the law of Moses in every part of daily life
decisions.reason: They were respected teachers among the people. They had grumbled when Jesus welcomed sinners (15:2).

decisions.choice: lovers of money: greedy
decisions.reason: The word describes a love of money, not wealth itself (2 Timothy 3:2). Jesus has just said that no one can serve both God and wealth.

decisions.choice: ridiculing: turning up the nose, sneering
decisions.reason: The verb comes from the word for a nose. It is used of the rulers mocking Jesus at the cross (23:35).

decisions.choice: turned up their noses at
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture in the Greek verb.

records.heading: Lovers of money

records.source: καὶ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Ὑμεῖς ἐστε οἱ δικαιοῦντες ἑαυτοὺς ἐνώπιον τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὁ δὲ θεὸς γινώσκει τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν· ὅτι τὸ ἐν ἀνθρώποις ὑψηλὸν βδέλυγμα ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ.
records.gloss: And he said to them, You are those justifying themselves before the men, but the God knows the hearts of you; for that which among men [is] exalted [is] an abomination before the God.
pieces: He said to them, "You are the ones who make yourselves out to be righteous in front of {{gender:people|men}}, but God knows your hearts. What {{gender:people|men}} think highly of is loathsome in God's sight.

L.15: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "You are the ones who justify yourselves before {{gender:people|men}}, but God knows your hearts; for what is exalted among {{gender:people|men}} is an abomination before God.

R.15: Jesus said to them, "You try to make {{gender:people|men}} think you are good. But God knows what is in your hearts. The things {{gender:people|men}} think are great are the very things God hates.

decisions.choice: justify yourselves: show yourselves to be in the right, make yourselves look righteous
decisions.reason: They seek to be seen as righteous by others (10:29; 18:9-14). God, who sees the heart, judges differently.

decisions.choice: God knows your hearts: the God who looks on the heart
decisions.reason: Scripture says that people look at outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Proverbs 21:2).

decisions.choice: abomination: something God finds disgusting
decisions.reason: The word is used in the Greek Old Testament for what the Lord hates, such as idols and the pride of the arrogant (Proverbs 16:5).

decisions.choice: exalted: high, prized, admired
decisions.reason: What people prize, such as wealth and a good name, can be the very thing God rejects (1:51-53).

decisions.choice: {{gender:people|men}}
decisions.reason: The word means human beings in general.

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and runs on to 16:31
decisions.reason: Jesus' words from 16:15 to the end of the chapter are one speech.

records.source: Ὁ νόμος καὶ οἱ προφῆται μέχρι Ἰωάννου· ἀπὸ τότε ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ εὐαγγελίζεται καὶ πᾶς εἰς αὐτὴν βιάζεται.
records.gloss: The law and the prophets [were] until John; from that time the kingdom of the God is proclaimed and everyone into it forces his way.
pieces: The law and the prophets lasted until John. From then on, the kingdom of God is announced as good news, and everyone is pressing their way into it.

L.16: The law and the prophets [were] until John; from that time the kingdom of God is proclaimed as good news, and everyone is forcing [a way] into it.

R.16: The law of Moses and the writings of the prophets were God's message until John came. Since then, the good news about the kingdom of God is being told. And people are pushing hard to get into it.

decisions.choice: the law and the prophets: the Scriptures of Israel
decisions.reason: The phrase names the whole Old Testament by two of its parts (24:27, 44).

decisions.choice: until John; from that time: John stands at the turn from the time of promise to the time of the kingdom
decisions.reason: The law and the prophets pointed ahead to what has now come (7:26-28). The next verse shows that the law has not lost its force.

decisions.choice: everyone is forcing a way into it: people press hard to enter
alternatives: everyone is urged to enter it
decisions.reason: The verb means to use force. It may describe the eagerness of those who enter (13:24), or, taken as a passive, people being urged to come in (14:23). Others take it of violent opposition. Matthew 11:12 has a related saying.

decisions.choice: is proclaimed as good news: is announced as news of salvation
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used for the good news Jesus brings (4:18, 43; 8:1).

decisions.choice: [were]; [a way]
decisions.reason: Literal supplies the verb and the object English needs.

decisions.choice: were God's message until John came
decisions.reason: Readable supplies what the law and the prophets were, as the meaning decisions explain.

records.source: Εὐκοπώτερον δέ ἐστιν τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν παρελθεῖν ἢ τοῦ νόμου μίαν κεραίαν πεσεῖν.
records.gloss: Easier however it is the heaven and the earth to pass away than of the law one stroke of a pen to fail.
pieces: Yet heaven and earth will pass away more easily than one tiny stroke of the law will fall away.

L.17: But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the law to fall.

R.17: But the whole world, heaven and earth, could more easily come to an end than the smallest part of the law could fail.

decisions.choice: stroke: a tiny mark that tells one letter from another
decisions.reason: The word means a little horn or hook, the small stroke on a letter. Not the least part of God's law will fail (Matthew 5:18).

decisions.choice: heaven and earth: the whole created world
alternatives: the sky and the ground only
decisions.reason: The pair names everything God has made (Genesis 1:1; Luke 21:33).

decisions.choice: to fall: to fail, to lose its force
decisions.reason: A word that falls is one that is not fulfilled or no longer holds.

decisions.choice: the smallest part
decisions.reason: Readable gives the meaning of the picture.

records.source: Πᾶς ὁ ἀπολύων τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ καὶ γαμῶν ἑτέραν μοιχεύει, καὶ ὁ ἀπολελυμένην ἀπὸ ἀνδρὸς γαμῶν μοιχεύει.
records.gloss: Everyone putting away the wife of him and marrying another commits adultery, and the [one] her having been put away from a husband marrying commits adultery.
pieces: Any man who divorces his wife and marries someone else is committing adultery, and the man who marries a woman her husband has divorced is committing adultery too.

L.18: Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and the one who marries a woman divorced from a husband commits adultery.

R.18: If a man divorces his wife and marries another woman, he is guilty of adultery. And if a man marries a woman whose husband has divorced her, he is also guilty of adultery.

decisions.choice: divorces: sends away, dismisses his wife
decisions.reason: The verb means to release or send away. In Jewish law a husband could divorce his wife by giving her a written notice (Deuteronomy 24:1-4).

decisions.choice: a saying that shows the law's force: marriage stays binding before God
alternatives: a new law replacing the law of Moses
decisions.reason: After saying that not a stroke of the law will fail (16:17), Jesus gives an example where he holds people to God's purpose for marriage more strictly than common practice (Mark 10:2-12; Matthew 19:3-9).

decisions.choice: the one who marries a woman divorced: the second man also breaks the marriage bond
decisions.reason: The subject is the man who marries her. Luke gives the saying from the side of the men, who alone could divorce under the law.

records.source: Ἄνθρωπος δέ τις ἦν πλούσιος, καὶ ἐνεδιδύσκετο πορφύραν καὶ βύσσον εὐφραινόμενος καθ’ ἡμέραν λαμπρῶς.
records.gloss: A man now certain there was rich, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, making good cheer every day in splendor.
pieces: There was once a rich man who wore purple and fine linen and feasted in great style day after day.

L.19: Now there was a certain rich man, and he used to dress in purple and fine linen, feasting splendidly every day.

R.19: There was once a rich man who always wore expensive purple robes and clothes made of fine linen. Every day he had grand meals and enjoyed himself.

decisions.choice: purple and fine linen: the clothing of kings and the very rich
decisions.reason: Purple dye came from shellfish and was very costly. Fine linen, often from Egypt, was worn next to the skin. Together they marked great wealth (Proverbs 31:22; Revelation 18:12).

decisions.choice: feasting splendidly every day: enjoying rich meals in luxury, day after day
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used for the celebration of 15:23-24 and the rich fool's "be merry" (12:19). Here it is a way of life.

decisions.choice: a certain rich man: the parable begins like the one in 16:1
decisions.reason: The words "a certain rich man" open both parables of this chapter (16:1). The rich man has no name.

records.heading: A rich man and a poor man named Lazarus

records.source: πτωχὸς δέ τις ὀνόματι Λάζαρος ἐβέβλητο πρὸς τὸν πυλῶνα αὐτοῦ εἱλκωμένος καὶ ἐπιθυμῶν χορτασθῆναι ἀπὸ τῶν πιπτόντων ἀπὸ τῆς τραπέζης τοῦ πλουσίου· ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ κύνες ἐρχόμενοι ἐπέλειχον τὰ ἕλκη αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: A poor man now certain named Lazarus was laid at the gate of him being full of sores \v 21 and desiring to be fed from the [things] falling from the table of the rich man; but even the dogs coming were licking the sores of him.
pieces: And a poor man named Lazarus had been put down at his gate. His body was covered with sores,
and he longed to fill his stomach with whatever dropped from the rich man's table. Instead, the dogs would come and lick his sores.

L.20: And a certain poor man named Lazarus had been laid at his gate, covered with sores,
L.21: and longing to be fed from what fell from the rich man's table; but even the dogs would come and lick his sores.

R.20: A poor man named Lazarus was lying by the gate of the rich man's house. Someone had put him there. Lazarus had sores all over his body.
R.21: He was so hungry that he wanted to eat even the scraps of food that fell from the rich man's table. Dogs even came and licked his sores.

decisions.choice: Lazarus: a common Jewish name, a form of Eleazar, meaning "God helps"
decisions.reason: He is the only person named in any of Jesus' parables. The name fits him: he has no one but God to help him.

decisions.choice: had been laid: placed there by others, because he could not walk or stand
decisions.reason: The verb means "thrown" or "put". Others had left him there to beg.

decisions.choice: what fell from the rich man's table (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "the crumbs", perhaps from Matthew 15:27. The earliest manuscripts do not have it. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: but even the dogs ... licked his sores: he was so helpless that stray dogs came to him
alternatives: the dogs were caring for him
decisions.reason: Dogs in the streets were scavengers and counted unclean. "But even" adds to his misery: no one fed him, and he could not keep the dogs away.

decisions.choice: Someone had put him there.
decisions.reason: Readable explains the passive, as the meaning decision explains.

decisions.choice: eat even the scraps of food
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what fell from the table.

records.source: ἐγένετο δὲ ἀποθανεῖν τὸν πτωχὸν καὶ ἀπενεχθῆναι αὐτὸν ὑπὸ τῶν ἀγγέλων εἰς τὸν κόλπον Ἀβραάμ· ἀπέθανεν δὲ καὶ ὁ πλούσιος καὶ ἐτάφη.
records.gloss: It came to pass then [that] died the poor man and was carried away he by the angels into the bosom of Abraham; died then also the rich man and was buried.
pieces: The day came when the poor man died, and angels carried him off to be at Abraham's side. The rich man also died, and was given a burial.

L.22: And it came about that the poor man died and was carried away by the angels into Abraham's bosom; and the rich man also died and was buried.

R.22: Then Lazarus died, and the angels carried him away to sit close beside Abraham. The rich man died too, and people buried him.

decisions.choice: into Abraham's bosom: to the place of honor beside Abraham
alternatives: Abraham held him like a child
decisions.reason: At a feast, guests reclined on couches, and the one closest to the host lay against his chest (John 13:23). Lazarus shares the feast of God's kingdom with Abraham, the father of Israel (13:28-29).

decisions.choice: was buried: the rich man had a proper burial, but nothing more is said
decisions.reason: Nothing is said of a burial for Lazarus, who is carried by angels. The rich man's story ends in a grave.

decisions.choice: carried by the angels: God's care for the poor man at his death
alternatives: a teaching about how every soul travels after death
decisions.reason: The parable uses pictures known from Jewish teaching of the time. Its point is the great reversal, not a map of the life after death.

decisions.choice: to be at Abraham's side (B); to sit close beside Abraham (R)
decisions.reason: "Bosom" is old-fashioned. Balanced and Readable give the sense of the picture, which Literal keeps.

decisions.choice: Lazarus
decisions.reason: Readable names him.

records.source: καὶ ἐν τῷ ᾅδῃ ἐπάρας τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτοῦ, ὑπάρχων ἐν βασάνοις, ὁρᾷ Ἀβραὰμ ἀπὸ μακρόθεν καὶ Λάζαρον ἐν τοῖς κόλποις αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: And in the Hades having lifted up the eyes of him, being in torments, he sees Abraham from afar and Lazarus in the bosom of him.
pieces: From Hades, in the midst of his torment, he raised his eyes and saw Abraham a long way off, and Lazarus close beside him.

L.23: And in Hades, lifting up his eyes, being in torment, he sees Abraham far off and Lazarus in his bosom.

R.23: The rich man went to the place of the dead and was in great pain there. He looked up and saw Abraham far away, with Lazarus right next to him.

decisions.choice: Hades: the place of the dead
decisions.reason: The Greek Old Testament uses the word for Sheol, the world of the dead (10:15; Acts 2:27). Here it is a place of torment for the rich man, separated from the place where Lazarus is. It is a different word from Gehenna (12:5).

decisions.choice: torment: severe pain
decisions.reason: The word is used of torture and severe pain (Matthew 4:24). 16:24 speaks of a flame.

decisions.choice: he sees: a vivid present in the middle of the story
decisions.reason: The storyteller switches to the present tense to make the scene come alive.

decisions.choice: saw (B, R); sees (L)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the past tense of the story.

decisions.choice: the place of the dead
decisions.reason: Readable explains Hades, as in 10:15.

decisions.choice: close beside him (B); right next to him (R)
decisions.reason: As in 16:22.

records.source: καὶ αὐτὸς φωνήσας εἶπεν· Πάτερ Ἀβραάμ, ἐλέησόν με καὶ πέμψον Λάζαρον ἵνα βάψῃ τὸ ἄκρον τοῦ δακτύλου αὐτοῦ ὕδατος καὶ καταψύξῃ τὴν γλῶσσάν μου, ὅτι ὀδυνῶμαι ἐν τῇ φλογὶ ταύτῃ.
records.gloss: And he having cried out said, Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus that he might dip the tip of the finger of him in water and cool the tongue of me, for I am suffering in the flame this.
pieces: So he shouted, 'Father Abraham, show me mercy! Send Lazarus here. Let him wet the end of his finger with water and cool my tongue, for this flame is causing me terrible pain.'

L.24: And he called out and said, 'Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in agony in this flame.'

R.24: So he called out, 'Father Abraham, please be kind to me! Send Lazarus to me. Let him put the end of his finger in some water and cool my tongue with it. I am suffering terribly in this fire!'

decisions.choice: Father Abraham: he claims Abraham as his ancestor
decisions.reason: Jews called Abraham their father (3:8; John 8:39). Abraham answers "child" (16:25), but being his descendant does not save the rich man.

decisions.choice: send Lazarus: he still treats Lazarus as someone to run errands for him
decisions.reason: He speaks to Abraham, not to Lazarus, and asks for Lazarus to be sent to serve him.

decisions.choice: I am in agony: in great pain and distress
decisions.reason: The verb is used of deep pain or grief (2:48; Acts 20:38).

decisions.choice: short sentences
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable break the request into short sentences.

records.source: εἶπεν δὲ Ἀβραάμ· Τέκνον, μνήσθητι ὅτι ἀπέλαβες τὰ ἀγαθά σου ἐν τῇ ζωῇ σου, καὶ Λάζαρος ὁμοίως τὰ κακά· νῦν δὲ ὧδε παρακαλεῖται σὺ δὲ ὀδυνᾶσαι.
records.gloss: Said then Abraham, Child, remember that you received fully the good [things] of you in the lifetime of you, and Lazarus likewise the evil [things]; now however here he is comforted, you however are suffering.
pieces: But Abraham answered, 'My child, remember: while you were alive you had your good things, and Lazarus in the same way had the bad things. Now here he finds comfort, and you are suffering.

L.25: But Abraham said, 'Child, remember that you received your good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise the bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in agony.

R.25: But Abraham said, 'My child, remember how you lived. You had plenty of good things in your life, and Lazarus had many bad things happen to him. Now he is comforted here, and you are in pain.

decisions.choice: you received: you received in full, and have nothing more to come
decisions.reason: The verb means to receive what is due, in full. Compare 6:24, where a related verb says that the rich have already received their comfort.

decisions.choice: now he is comforted, and you are in agony: the great reversal
alternatives: a rule that all rich people suffer
decisions.reason: Mary's song (1:52-53) and the blessings and woes (6:20-26) speak of the same turning of fortunes. The rich man's fault is shown in 16:19-21: he feasted while Lazarus starved at his gate.

decisions.choice: your good things; the bad things: the rich man's good things were his own choice and possession
decisions.reason: Abraham says "your good things", but only "the bad things" of Lazarus.

decisions.choice: Abraham's words open here and run on to 16:26
decisions.reason: Abraham's answer is one speech.

records.source: καὶ ἐν πᾶσι τούτοις μεταξὺ ἡμῶν καὶ ὑμῶν χάσμα μέγα ἐστήρικται, ὅπως οἱ θέλοντες διαβῆναι ἔνθεν πρὸς ὑμᾶς μὴ δύνωνται, μηδὲ ἐκεῖθεν πρὸς ἡμᾶς διαπερῶσιν.
records.gloss: And besides all these things between us and you a chasm great has been fixed, so that those desiring to pass from here to you not are able, nor from there to us can they cross over.
pieces: What is more, a vast gulf lies fixed between us and you. Anyone who wanted to go across from here to you could not, and no one can cross from your side to ours.'

L.26: And besides all these things, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, so that those who want to pass from here to you are not able, nor may they cross over from there to us.'

R.26: Besides, there is a huge, deep gap between us and you. It is there so that no one from here can cross over to you, even if they want to. And no one from there can cross over to us.'

decisions.choice: a great chasm has been fixed: a wide gap that cannot be crossed, set in place for good
decisions.reason: The verb means firmly set. The passive implies that God set it there. The choices of this life cannot be undone after death.

decisions.choice: besides all these things: in addition to what I have said
decisions.reason: Abraham gives a second reason why Lazarus cannot be sent.

decisions.choice: those who want to pass from here: even those who would like to go and help
decisions.reason: Abraham does not say that no one in his place has pity. The way is closed even to those who might want to cross.

decisions.choice: a vast gulf (B); a huge, deep gap (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use everyday words for the gap.

records.source: εἶπεν δέ· Ἐρωτῶ σε οὖν, πάτερ, ἵνα πέμψῃς αὐτὸν εἰς τὸν οἶκον τοῦ πατρός μου, ἔχω γὰρ πέντε ἀδελφούς, ὅπως διαμαρτύρηται αὐτοῖς, ἵνα μὴ καὶ αὐτοὶ ἔλθωσιν εἰς τὸν τόπον τοῦτον τῆς βασάνου.
records.gloss: He said then, I implore you then, father, that you would send him to the house of the father of me, \v 28 I have for five brothers, so that he might warn them, that not also they might come to the place this of torment.
pieces: 'Then, father, I ask you this,' he said. 'Send him to my father's house,
where I have five brothers. He can give them a solemn warning, so that they do not come to this place of torment as well.'

L.27: And he said, 'Then I ask you, father, to send him to my father's house,
L.28: for I have five brothers, so that he may warn them, so that they also may not come to this place of torment.'

R.27: The rich man said, 'Then please, father, send Lazarus to my father's house.
R.28: I have five brothers there. Let Lazarus warn them, so that they will not come to this place of pain too.'

decisions.choice: warn: testify to them, give them a solemn warning
decisions.reason: The verb means to bear witness with earnestness. In Acts it is used of the apostles' witness (Acts 2:40; 20:21).

decisions.choice: my father's house: his family, the household he grew up in
decisions.reason: "House" means the household and family.

decisions.choice: I ask you: he still asks for Lazarus to be sent on an errand
decisions.reason: As in 16:24, he speaks to Abraham about Lazarus. He now cares for his brothers, but still treats Lazarus as a messenger for his family.

decisions.choice: Lazarus
decisions.reason: Readable names the man to be sent.

records.source: λέγει δὲ Ἀβραάμ· Ἔχουσι Μωϋσέα καὶ τοὺς προφήτας· ἀκουσάτωσαν αὐτῶν.
records.gloss: Says however Abraham, They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.
pieces: But Abraham said, 'Moses and the prophets are there for them. Let your brothers listen to what they say.'

L.29: But Abraham says, 'They have Moses and the prophets; let them listen to them.'

R.29: But Abraham said, 'Your brothers have the books that Moses and the prophets wrote. They should listen to them.'

decisions.choice: Moses and the prophets: the Scriptures of Israel
decisions.reason: Moses stands for the law, the first part of the Scriptures (16:16; 24:27). They already warn against neglecting the poor (Deuteronomy 15:7-11; Isaiah 58:6-7).

decisions.choice: let them listen: let them hear and obey
decisions.reason: To listen to God's word is to do what it says (8:21; 11:28).

decisions.choice: said (B, R); says (L)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the past tense of the story.

decisions.choice: the books that Moses and the prophets wrote
decisions.reason: Readable explains the phrase, as the meaning decision explains.

records.source: ὁ δὲ εἶπεν· Οὐχί, πάτερ Ἀβραάμ, ἀλλ’ ἐάν τις ἀπὸ νεκρῶν πορευθῇ πρὸς αὐτοὺς μετανοήσουσιν.
records.gloss: He and said, No, father Abraham, but if one from [the] dead should go to them, they will repent.
pieces: He answered, 'That is not enough, father Abraham. But if someone goes to them from among the dead, they will repent.'

L.30: And he said, 'No, father Abraham; but if someone from the dead goes to them, they will repent.'

R.30: The rich man said, 'No, father Abraham, they will not listen. But if someone comes back from the dead and goes to them, they will turn away from their sins.'

decisions.choice: No: they will not listen to Moses and the prophets alone
alternatives: No, I do not agree that they have them
decisions.reason: He does not deny that they have the Scriptures; he says that will not be enough.

decisions.choice: repent: turn from sin back to God
decisions.reason: As in 15:7.

decisions.choice: That is not enough (B); they will not listen (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the "no" refers to, as the meaning decision explains.

decisions.choice: turn away from their sins
decisions.reason: Readable explains the word, as in 11:32.

records.source: εἶπεν δὲ αὐτῷ· Εἰ Μωϋσέως καὶ τῶν προφητῶν οὐκ ἀκούουσιν, οὐδ’ ἐάν τις ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῇ πεισθήσονται.
records.gloss: He said however to him, If Moses and the prophets not they hear, not even if one out from [the] dead should rise will they be persuaded.
pieces: Abraham said to him, 'If they will not listen to Moses and the prophets, then even someone rising from the dead will not persuade them.'"

L.31: But he said to him, 'If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded if someone rises from the dead.'"

R.31: Abraham said to him, 'If your brothers will not listen to Moses and the prophets, they will not be convinced even if someone comes back to life from the dead.'"

decisions.choice: if someone rises from the dead: pointing ahead to Jesus' own resurrection
decisions.reason: The words fit what Luke goes on to tell: Jesus rose from the dead, and even then many were not persuaded. The risen Jesus explains himself from Moses and all the prophets (24:25-27, 44-46).

decisions.choice: will be persuaded: will be convinced and change their ways
decisions.reason: The verb means to be won over. A sign from the dead will not change a heart that will not hear God's word.

decisions.choice: rises: is raised to life
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used for rising from the dead (18:33; 24:7, 46). It is stronger than "goes to them" in 16:30.

decisions.choice: Abraham
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker.

decisions.choice: Abraham's words and Jesus' speech close here
decisions.reason: The parable ends with the chapter.
